ch55.anchor: later he served the new government as head of the College of Engineering
ch55.note: Ōtori Keisuke (1833–1911) was born the son of a village doctor in Akō, and rose through Dutch and then French military studies to command the shogunate’s Western-drilled infantry. He led the shogunal die-hards north in this campaign, fought on to Hakodate, and after the war built the long official career Shiba lists here: the Imperial College of Engineering, the Peers’ School, the legation to Qing China, the Privy Council, a barony. With Enomoto, he was one of the few leaders of the losing side to prosper under the government that had beaten him.

ch55.anchor: the Ogata Kōan academy in Osaka
ch55.note: Rangaku, “Dutch learning,” was the study of Western science and arts through the Dutch, the one European nation allowed to trade at Nagasaki during the country’s long seclusion. Ogata Kōan’s academy in Osaka, the Tekijuku, was its most famous school; from it came many of the physicians, soldiers, and reformers who carried Western knowledge into the last shogunal decade and on into the Meiji state.

ch55.anchor: Katsu Kaishū and Ōkubo Ichiō above all
ch55.note: Ōkubo Ichiō (1817–1888) was a senior Tokugawa official and, with Katsu Kaishū, a leading voice of the party that chose submission and the peaceful surrender of Edo over a fight to the finish. To such men the Shinsengumi, still spoiling for war inside the capital, were an embarrassment; the money they gave Kondō for the Kōshū expedition was, Shiba suggests here, in part to be rid of them.

Goryō-hei were soldiers raised from the tenryō, the shogunate’s own demesne, the lands it held directly rather than granting them to a daimyō. With the Tokugawa house fallen, these were among the last troops still answering to it.

ch55.anchor: the festival day of the Tōshōgū
ch55.note: The Tōshōgū is the shrine at Nikkō where Tokugawa Ieyasu, deified as the god Toshō-Daigongen, is enshrined; the seventeenth of the fourth month was the anniversary of his death and the shrine’s great festival. To win a battle on that very day struck Ōtori as a portent that Ieyasu’s house would rise again.
